text: Brennick Retail Holdings is a fictional mid-size retail chain, used here to walk through a pattern this course already named back in Chapter two. It is not a real company, and nothing in this case study describes an actual reported incident -- it's a composite scenario, built to make a cost mechanism easier to see than a bullet list of risks ever could.

Three years ago, a new VP of Infrastructure arrived with a simple conviction: never be locked into one cloud provider. That became architectural law, applied everywhere at once, with no cost model backing it up front. Every new system, regardless of what it actually did, had to run on both Azure and AWS, ideally deployed to both simultaneously, adopted as a principle rather than evaluated as a tradeoff.

None of what followed was one bad decision -- it was four ordinary ones that compounded. Every platform team maintained two of everything, from monitoring to policy to deployment pipelines, with no shared learning curve between them. Hiring roughly doubled, since every role needed comfort in two clouds' identity and networking models instead of one. And replicating data between clouds to keep local copies current turned recurring egress fees into one of the largest line items on the entire infrastructure budget.

The stated goal was pricing leverage and protection against a single-provider outage. Neither materialized at anywhere near the scale of the cost. Brennick's actual volume wasn't large enough to extract real pricing leverage, and in three years there was no single-provider outage the architecture meaningfully protected against. The insurance premium was being paid every single month; the claim it was insuring against essentially never came.

Most tellingly, the majority of Brennick's systems -- internal reporting tools, a handful of marketing microsites, an HR portal -- had no real multi-cloud requirement at all, yet paid the full duplicated cost anyway, because the policy never distinguished between workloads. The actual fix was never banning multi-cloud. It was evaluating lock-in risk per workload, the way Lesson eight recommended, and reserving deliberate duplication for the few systems with a real, costed case for it.

Two labs built hybrid and multi-cloud architecture deliberately, for a named requirement. This case study showed the same tools reached for by default, with no requirement and no cost model, and what that actually costs over three years. Lesson thirty-two closes the chapter, and the whole course, by pulling all eight chapters together through the lens of these three lessons.
